rationale: Start with a broad, moderately fast gradient to locate all six compounds while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained components. The retention window and critical resolutions will guide subsequent slope, solvent-window, and temperature adjustments.
The first injection already achieved the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved separation, using the substantial resolution margin.
Shorten the gradient another grid step while keeping solvent endpoints and temperature fixed. The minimum resolution of 3.24 provides room to reduce separation time while retaining the maximum CRF.
Test the next shorter gradient; the observed trend suggests the critical first pair may remain above R = 1.5. This could further reduce separation time while preserving the maximum CRF.

Test the minimum gradient duration to establish the speed–resolution boundary; the first pair is likely to fall below R = 1.5. The 4-minute gradient remains the fastest validated method with maximum CRF.

Return to the shortest fully resolved gradient and raise temperature to test whether elution can be accelerated without losing the critical first-pair resolution. Keep the 40 C method as the validated maximum-CRF fallback.

Test a gentler 2-minute gradient at lower temperature to recover first-pair resolution, since heating worsened that pair. The final-solvent hold may still elute the last compound faster than the validated 4-minute method.

Raise the final organic fraction one grid step to accelerate the last peak during the hold. The critical first-pair resolution may approach 1.5, testing whether this shorter gradient can retain maximum CRF with a faster last elution.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to reduce the gradient slope while retaining the stronger final solvent. Test whether this restores the marginal first-pair resolution to at least 1.5 without sacrificing the faster last-peak elution.

Shift both solvent endpoints upward one step, preserving the slope that gave full resolution in injection 9. This should accelerate the last peak while testing whether the earlier peaks retain adequate resolution.

Shift both endpoints upward another grid step while preserving gradient slope and temperature. Injection 10 maintained first-pair resolution, so this tests a further reduction in last-peak retention while targeting CRF 1.000.

Shift both endpoints upward one more step, reaching the maximum final organic fraction while preserving gradient slope. This should further shorten last-peak retention, with first-pair resolution checked as the early peaks approach the dead time.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step while keeping the maximum final strength and minimum gradient duration. This tests whether a narrower solvent window further accelerates elution while preserving full resolution of the early pair.
Raise temperature one grid step to accelerate the last peak while testing the first pair’s improved resolution margin. Keep the solvent window fixed to isolate the temperature effect.

Test one higher starting organic fraction to seek faster elution at the current temperature. The first pair is approaching the pre-gradient elution region, so this injection will establish whether early-peak compression limits further solvent-window narrowing.

Return to the validated starting composition and test one higher temperature to locate the thermal resolution boundary. The first pair may fall below 1.5; injection 14 remains the fastest validated maximum-CRF method.

Test whether cooling restores full resolution at the higher starting organic fraction, completing the local temperature–composition comparison. Injection 14 remains the fastest validated method achieving the maximum CRF.

Lower the final organic fraction one step to test a gentler gradient with more first-pair resolution margin than injection 14. This seeks a nearby maximum-CRF alternative with stronger resolution, accepting a modest increase in last-peak retention.

Cool the latest fully resolved method one step to seek greater critical-pair resolution margin while keeping elution near three minutes. The maximum CRF is already secured; injection 14 remains the fastest validated method achieving it.

Lower the starting organic fraction one step from injection 18 to test a nearby fully resolved method with later early-peak elution. This refines the maximum-CRF operating region while retaining injection 14 as the fastest validated option.

Cool injection 20 by one grid step to increase its narrow first-pair resolution margin while keeping the separation short. This tests another nearby maximum-CRF option; injection 14 remains the fastest validated fully resolved method.

Test the remaining immediate lower-starting-organic neighbor of injection 14 to complete the local speed–resolution comparison. First-pair resolution may be marginal; injection 14 remains the fastest validated method with CRF 1.000.

Test a lower starting organic fraction at the cooler temperature, where the observed slope trend predicts first-pair resolution just above 1.5. This seeks another fast maximum-CRF method with early peaks farther from the dead time; injection 14 remains the fastest validated option.

Reduce the final organic fraction from injection 21 to increase the critical-pair resolution margin while keeping all peaks well within ten minutes. This targets another maximum-CRF alternative; injection 14 remains the fastest validated fully resolved method.

Raise temperature one step from injection 24 to shorten elution while using its first-pair resolution margin to preserve maximum CRF. Injection 14 remains the fastest validated maximum-CRF method, with the last peak at 2.58 minutes.
